newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish unions lock arms against EMU wage freeze.
newsitem.headline: Spanish unions lock arms against EMU wage freeze.

text.p: Spain's major trade unions joined forces on Tuesday against a freeze on public-sector wages intended to help whip the country's finances into shape for Europe's planned economic and monetary union (EMU).

Unions called on two million workers who stand to be hit by the freeze to demonstrate in regional capitals from 7.00 p.m. (1700 GMT) in what was expected to be the largest mass protest since the Popular Party (PP) took office in May.

With the ink still wet on a pensions deal between the unions and the new conservative administration, the protest shows labour leaders are involved in an uneasy love-hate relationship with the government of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar.
They have succeeded in striking a deal guaranteeing the purchasing power and future payment of pensions which employer organisations denounced as over-generous and refused to sign.
But they are digging in their heels on a wage freeze the government calls irreversible. Unions have warned they could call a general strike later this year if the freeze is not revoked.

"It is a fundamental objective for unions that there be no freeze on public-sector wages," said Dolores Liceras, employment secretary at Workers' Commissions (CCOO), one of Spain's two biggest unions.

The unions, led by CCOO and the General Workers' Union (UGT), say the measure violates an agreement with the previous Socialist administration which guaranteed wages would rise in line with inflation in 1997.
Public-sector workers have lost 11.2 percent of their buying power since 1993, saving the government 785 billion pesetas ($6.07 billion) in the process, according to the labour leaders.
"We're wondering what sacrifices they are asking of capital and company taxes," said Domingo Fernandez of the Confederation of Independent and Public Sector Unions (CSI-CSIF).
"We can't see any. On the contrary, they are granting them around half a trillion pesetas in capital gains."
The government says the wage freeze is needed as part of an austere 1997 draft budget aimed at bringing Spain's deficit down to the level required to join EMU in 1999.
It estimates the measure will slash 200 billion pesetas off the deficit, helping to bring it down to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997 from a forecast 4.4 percent in 1996.
The protest will remind Aznar that while he may have scored a small victory with the pensions deal signed last Wednesday, he still faces hurdles on the labour front in the coming year.
Analysts say Spanish unions cannot wield the power displayed by their French counterparts in mass strikes last year. The last general strike, in 1994, was widely considered a failure.
But Aznar could yet trip up on the issue of labour reform, due to be tackled next year.

Shortly after taking office, he said his priority was to reach a German-style jobs pact with unions against Spain's unemployment rate of almost 23 percent. Early talks with unions and employers failed, however, and the issue has been put on the back-burner.

Future talks will now have to overcome employer irritation over pensions talks, while financial markets would frown on the government giving in to unions on key issues such as making it cheaper to fire workers. ($1=129.3 Peseta)
